intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives a way to remember it and warns where people slip. Work the section exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and keep the latest NFHS fact sheet for your state open beside you.

sections.title: Malnutrition in all its forms
sections.big_idea: Malnutrition is **too little, too much or the wrong mix**. Stunting, wasting and underweight measure different things on different time scales.
in_plain_words: Public health uses malnutrition as an umbrella for three families of problem: undernutrition, micronutrient deficiency and overweight with diet-related disease. UNICEF calls their coexistence the triple burden. A child can be normal in size and still lack iron or vitamin A.

Each index reads differently. Height-for-age shows chronic deprivation, weight-for-height shows recent crisis, and weight-for-age mixes both. Stunting is a population indicator that records a child's history, so one short child proves little while a district where a third are short has a problem.

key_terms.meaning: Height-for-age below −2 SD of the WHO median; severe below −3 SD.
Weight-for-height below −2 SD, or MUAC under 125 mm, or oedema.
Weight-for-age below −2 SD; mixes chronic and acute problems.
Micronutrient deficiency that is invisible without a blood or urine test.
Undernutrition and overweight present together in a country, home or person.

worked_example.title: Classify four children
worked_example.setup: Use the z-score bands from the deck. Illustrative children: A has height-for-age −2.5, B has −3.2, C has weight-for-height −2.2, D has height-for-age −0.4 and weight-for-height −2.6.
steps: A is below −2 but not below −3: moderately stunted.
B is below −3: severely stunted.
C is below −2 on weight-for-height: wasted.
D has normal height but is wasted, so a stunting-only survey would miss D.
The NFHS drop in stunting is 35.5 − 29.3 = 6.2 points.
In relative terms, 6.2 ÷ 35.5 = 0.175, about 17.5 percent.
worked_example.answer: A moderately stunted, B severely stunted, C wasted, D wasted only. Stunting fell 6.2 points, about 17.5 percent in relative terms.

mistakes: Reading underweight as a measure of chronic hunger. It mixes stunting and wasting, so report all three indicators.
Judging a single short child as malnourished from height alone. Stunting is a population indicator.
Designing a programme to add calories only. A sugary ration can worsen the second burden.

recall.q: What z-score defines stunting and severe stunting?
recall.a: Height-for-age below −2 SD, and below −3 SD for severe.

recall.q: Which indicator tracks recent events such as a lean season?
recall.a: Wasting, because weight responds within weeks.

recall.q: What is the triple burden?
recall.a: Undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies and overweight, often in the same country, district or household.

recall.q: What was India's NFHS-6 stunting rate?
recall.a: 29.3 percent, down from 35.5 percent in NFHS-5.

recall.q: Why are the 2013 Lancet global numbers called a decade old by design?
recall.a: They come from the series that set the agenda, so use the latest Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates for current counts.

sections.title: Measuring malnutrition: standards, z-scores and the field
sections.big_idea: A nutrition number is only as good as its **yardstick, measurer and method**, so name all three whenever you quote a figure.
in_plain_words: The WHO 2006 standard describes how children grow when their needs are met. A z-score counts how far a child is from the healthy median. Cut-offs turn the score into yes or no, which loses information, so report the mean z-score with prevalence.

Error enters through age, position, equipment, measurer and recording, so standardise before fieldwork. MUAC offers a quick field screen, IYCF indicators describe diets, and anaemia depends on blood, device, adjustment and cut-off. Analyse surveys with weights and clusters, and protect child data.

key_terms.meaning: Number of standard deviations from the median for the same age and sex.
Mid-upper arm circumference, a tape used to screen for acute malnutrition.
Severe and moderate acute malnutrition.
Infant and young child feeding indicators from WHO and UNICEF.
Training exercise that tests each measurer's precision and accuracy.

worked_example.title: How the tool changes the caseload
worked_example.setup: Illustrative district of 10,000 children aged 6-59 months. Use the CNNS rates from slide 18: 17% wasted by weight-for-height, 5% by absolute MUAC below 125 mm.
steps: By weight-for-height: 10,000 × 0.17 = 1,700.
The tools pick overlapping but different children, so planning on one alone misjudges the caseload.
In a healthy population about 2.3% fall below −2 SD by chance: 10,000 × 0.023 = 230.
worked_example.answer: The weight-for-height caseload is 1,700 against 500 by MUAC, and about 230 children would fall below −2 SD by chance alone.

mistakes: Comparing trends measured on different yardsticks. Recompute on the WHO 2006 standard first.
Comparing anaemia figures without checking blood sample, device, adjustments and cut-off.
Treating a programme's own baseline as clean. Poor anthropometry there often creates a fake trend.

recall.q: When was the WHO Child Growth Standard released?
recall.a: 27 April 2006.

recall.q: How is a child under two measured?
recall.a: Lying down, for length, on a measuring board.

recall.q: What MUAC value marks severe acute malnutrition?
recall.a: Below 115 mm.

recall.q: By what number must DHS weights be divided?
When do the core DPDP duties apply?
recall.a: From 13 May 2027.

sections.title: Causes: the UNICEF frameworks and the first 1,000 days
sections.big_idea: Causes run from **diet and disease to food, care and power**, and damage begins early: before birth and by age two.
in_plain_words: The 1990 UNICEF framework sorts causes into immediate (diet and disease), underlying (food, care, health services) and basic (social, economic and cultural). The 2020 version asks what has to be in place and names the triple burden. Both warn that no single input is enough.

Direct nutrition-specific actions avert only about a fifth of stunting at very high coverage, so nutrition-sensitive action on income, sanitation and women's status carries the rest. Growth faltering starts in the womb, climbs steeply to 18-23 months, and links to a mother's schooling and gut infections.

key_terms.meaning: Inadequate dietary intake and disease.
Inadequate food, care or health services.
Acts on immediate determinants, such as supplements or counselling.
Acts on underlying causes, such as social protection or WASH.
Gut inflammation from faecal contamination that reduces absorption.

worked_example.title: Place each cause and size the gap
worked_example.setup: Place four causes on the framework, then size what direct action leaves undone. Illustrative: a district has 1,000 stunted children.
steps: Low dietary intake is immediate. A broken health post is underlying.
Poverty and gender inequality are basic causes.
Ten direct interventions at very high coverage avert about a fifth: 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200.
Stunted children left: 1,000 − 200 = 800.
Those 800 depend on income, sanitation, women's status and food prices.
worked_example.answer: Direct interventions would avert about 200 of 1,000 stunted children and leave about 800 to wider change in other sectors.

mistakes: Starting a stunting programme at six months. Growth faltering often begins in the womb.
Reading the education gradient as a causal sum. Schooling, wealth and residence overlap.
Dropping the basic causes to avoid politics. Jonsson criticised that, and you can work at one level while naming the others.

recall.q: What three levels does the 1990 framework use?
recall.a: Immediate, underlying and basic causes.

recall.q: Which window counts as the first 1,000 days?
recall.a: Conception to the second birthday.

recall.q: What share of infants under 6 months is already stunted?
recall.a: About 24.4 percent.

recall.q: How much less likely is a stunted child when the mother has 12 or more years of schooling?
recall.a: About half as likely as when the mother has none.

recall.q: Why can a well-fed child still falter?
recall.a: A gut inflamed by faecal contamination reduces absorption.

sections.title: India's numbers: NFHS and CNNS
sections.big_idea: NFHS gives the trend and the CNNS gives the **micronutrient and older-child picture**. Stunting is falling, and wasting and anaemia are not.
in_plain_words: NFHS-6 (2023-24) reports 29.3 percent stunted, 19.0 wasted and 31.8 underweight, from a provisional fact sheet. Stunting has fallen across four rounds while wasting has stayed near 19 to 21 percent. Anaemia rose between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5, and no newer figure had been released by October 2026.

The CNNS of 2016-18 measured children and adolescents up to 19 and tested blood and urine. It shows iron deficiency and anaemia overlap without matching, and that adolescent girls are the missing middle of policy. Feeding data show exclusive breastfeeding falling and diets inadequate.

diagram.caption: stunting in India, children under five

key_terms.meaning: National Family Health Survey, India's Demographic and Health Survey.
National nutrition survey of 2016-18, with blood and urine samples.
NFHS-6 fact sheet values awaiting the full report.
Blood marker used to measure iron deficiency.
Position of a child among siblings; stunting rises with it.

worked_example.title: How fast did stunting fall?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's national rates for children under five and the round gaps it gives (about ten years, then about four years).
steps: NFHS-3 to NFHS-4: 48.0 − 38.4 = 9.6 points.
Per year over about ten years: 9.6 ÷ 10 = 0.96.
NFHS-5 to NFHS-6: 35.5 − 29.3 = 6.2 points.
Per year over about four years: 6.2 ÷ 4 = 1.55.
worked_example.answer: Stunting fell under a point a year, then roughly 1.5 points a year to NFHS-6, which matches the deck's own description.

mistakes: Quoting NFHS-6 anaemia. The fact sheets carry no anaemia indicator and the data had not been released by October 2026.
Using NFHS-6 for breakdowns by wealth or birth order. Those come from NFHS-5 until the NFHS-6 report appears.
Announcing a district's progress from a three-point change. District samples are small, so read the interval.

recall.q: How many households did NFHS-6 cover and which state was excluded?
recall.a: 679,238 households in every state and UT except Manipur.

recall.q: What did NFHS-5 find on child anaemia?
recall.a: 67.1 percent of children aged 6-59 months.

recall.q: What was the exclusive breastfeeding rate in NFHS-6?
recall.a: 55.8 percent, down from 63.7 percent.

recall.q: How many children and adolescents did the CNNS measure?
recall.a: 112,316, aged 0-19, in 30 states.

recall.q: Which groups does the CNNS cover that NFHS does not measure as children?
recall.a: School-age children (5-9) and adolescents (10-19).

sections.title: The Indian enigma debates
sections.big_idea: Experts argue about **why levels are high and whether they are measured right**, but the gradients that tell you who to reach hold under every yardstick.
in_plain_words: Indian children are on average shorter than children in sub-Saharan Africa, a poorer region. Four explanations compete: the yardstick overstates stunting, later-born children get less, open defecation harms growth, and maternal status sets the start. They can all be partly right.

The anaemia debate is similar. Cut-offs may be too high, and capillary blood gives higher prevalence than venous blood. Treat the debate as a question about levels. Gradients by wealth, birth order, schooling and sex among adolescents survive, so design for them now.

diagram.caption: four explanations that can all hold at once

key_terms.meaning: Shorter children in South Asia than in poorer African countries.
Finger or heel prick sample used by NFHS.
Sample from a vein, used by the CNNS.
The haemoglobin or z-score line that defines the condition.
Gradual improvement that arrives from outside any single programme.

worked_example.title: How much can method move a figure?
worked_example.setup: Compare the deck's figures where a change of method changes the level, then read one slope from Spears's district evidence.
steps: Stunting crude against standardised for 67 countries: 27.8 − 23.3 = 4.5 points.
CNNS anaemia on WHO cut-offs against Sachdev's cut-offs: 30.0 − 10.8 = 19.2 points.
NFHS child anaemia against the venous CNNS figure: 67.1 ÷ 30.7 = 2.19.
Spears: each 10% rise in open defecation goes with 0.7 points more stunting. Three such steps: 3 × 0.7 = 2.1.
worked_example.answer: Method moves levels by 4.5 to 19 points, and NFHS reads more than twice the CNNS. Spears's slope puts three 10% steps in open defecation near 2.1 points more stunting.

mistakes: Choosing a side before asking what changes if the critic is right. Often the level falls and the trend stays.
Treating Spears's district results as proof. The authors call them observational and ecological.
Adjusting for maternal height without noting that it reflects the mother's own childhood nutrition.

recall.q: Who dubbed the pattern the South Asian Enigma?
recall.a: Ramalingaswami and colleagues in 1996, as recounted by Pande.

recall.q: What did Jayachandran and Pande find about birth order?
recall.a: India's height gap relative to Africa grows sharply with birth order, linked to favouritism toward eldest sons.

recall.q: What share of height variation does sanitation explain in Spears's 140 country-years?
recall.a: 54 percent.

recall.q: When did WHO publish its revised haemoglobin cut-off guideline?
recall.a: 5 March 2024.

recall.q: What should you state next to any anaemia figure?
recall.a: The standard, the blood sample type and the cut-off.

sections.title: The right to food: NFSA 2013 and the PDS
sections.big_idea: Food is a **legal entitlement** in India, with grain, meals and cash for mothers, and routes of complaint when they fail.
in_plain_words: A 2001 petition in PUCL v Union of India led the Supreme Court to turn food schemes into entitlements, and the NFSA 2013 wrote them into law. Priority households get 5 kg per person per month, Antyodaya households 35 kg, and PMGKAY has made the grain free since 2024.

Sections 4 to 6 add meals and maternity benefit across the life cycle. Section 13 puts the card in a woman's name, and section 8 gives an allowance when supply fails. Complaints climb from helplines to the State Food Commission. Digitisation and One Nation One Ration Card changed the PDS, and four debates remain.

events.what: PUCL petition on the right to food
One Nation One Ration Card begins
Cabinet approves five years of free grain

key_terms.meaning: Act making grain, meals and maternity benefit legal entitlements.
Antyodaya Anna Yojana households, entitled to 35 kg per household.
Scheme giving free foodgrain to about 81.35 crore people.
District Grievance Redressal Officer under s15.
One Nation One Ration Card, allowing inter-state portability.

worked_example.title: A household's monthly entitlement
worked_example.setup: Illustrative priority household with 5 members, using the NFSA numbers from slide 53.
steps: Grain: 5 × 5 = 25 kg a month.
At the Schedule I price of Rs 3 a kg for rice: 25 × 3 = 75 rupees.
An Antyodaya household gets 35 kg: 35 − 25 = 10 kg more.
State coverage illustration: 80 lakh rural people at up to 75% gives 80 × 0.75 = 60 lakh.
With 20 lakh urban people at up to 50%: 20 × 0.5 = 10 lakh.
worked_example.answer: The household draws 25 kg for Rs 75 at the rice price, and an Antyodaya household draws 10 kg more. The illustrative State could cover up to 70 lakh people.

mistakes: Treating grievance routes as working because they exist. The deck says their functioning varies widely.
Assuming free cereal fixes diets. It guarantees calories, and diversity needs pulses, oils, eggs and millets.
Skipping the ration card audit. Check whose name is on the card and whether the allowance was paid.

recall.q: What are the s3 entitlements?
recall.a: 5 kg per person per month for priority households and 35 kg per Antyodaya household.

recall.q: What does s13 provide?
recall.a: The eldest woman aged 18 or above is head of household for the ration card.

recall.q: What does s8 provide?
recall.a: A food security allowance from the State if grain or meals are not supplied.

recall.q: How many people does PMGKAY cover and until when?
recall.a: About 81.35 crore people, to 31 December 2028.

recall.q: What does the s16 body do?
recall.a: The State Food Commission monitors implementation and hears appeals.

sections.title: Programmes for mothers and children
sections.big_idea: India's programmes cover every stage of the life cycle, but children are lost at **each step from eligibility to effect**.
in_plain_words: ICDS began in 1975 and was merged into Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 in 2021-22. POSHAN Abhiyaan brought convergence and a tracker, PMMVY pays the maternity benefit and PM POSHAN serves school meals. Ministries share the work, so convergence at district level depends on one shared household list.

The delivery cascade is the main lens: eligible, enrolled, served, consumed, effective. Each arrow loses people, and monitoring that counts only the first two steps reports success while children stay short. Technology such as face recognition can add a new exclusion point.

key_terms.meaning: Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, merged in 2021-22.
App for Anganwadi attendance, rations and monthly growth data.
Food sent home for children under three and mothers.
Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana, a cash maternity benefit.
Different ministries working from one list of households.

worked_example.title: Trace the cascade
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 1,000 eligible children. Assume 80% enrol, 90% of those are served and 70% of those children actually eat the ration. Then check PMMVY's average payment.
steps: PMMVY average payout: 20,060 ÷ 4.26 = 4,709 rupees a beneficiary, since both figures are in crore.
The legal floor is Rs 6,000, so ask whether payments are partial.
worked_example.answer: About half the eligible children (504 of 1,000) end up eating the food. PMMVY's average of Rs 4,709 is below the Rs 6,000 floor, which is a question to ask.

mistakes: Counting enrolment as success. Consumption and effect come later in the cascade.
Assuming a take home ration is eaten by the child. It can be shared or sold.
Quoting PM POSHAN outlay without checking the current approval. The approved period ended with 2025-26.

recall.q: When was ICDS launched?
recall.a: 2 October 1975.

recall.q: What are the three verticals of Poshan 2.0?
recall.a: Nutrition support, early childhood care and education, and Anganwadi infrastructure.

recall.q: What was POSHAN Abhiyaan's ambition for stunting?
recall.a: To fall from 38.4 percent to 25 percent by 2022.

recall.q: Which section of the NFSA holds the school meal entitlement?
recall.a: Section 5(1)(b).

recall.q: What is the practical test of convergence at district level?
recall.a: Whether the Anganwadi Worker, ASHA, ANM and fair price shop dealer share one list of households and meet on a fixed day.

sections.title: Anaemia, micronutrients and fortification
sections.big_idea: Anaemia has **several causes**, so the response must be matched to the cause, and fortification works best where one cheap nutrient suits one staple.
in_plain_words: Anemia Mukt Bharat uses six groups, six interventions and six mechanisms, including iron folic acid and deworming. The CNNS shows iron deficiency explains only part of anaemia, so a single-cause programme will plateau. Track tablets taken, test reliably and screen for haemoglobin disorders.

Fortification is regulated by the 2018 FSSAI rules. Rice fortification now reaches all government schemes, with a debate over benefit and the sickle cell advisory. Iodised salt shows how fortification can succeed. Eat Right India addresses the other half of the double burden.

events.what: Phased rollout, ICDS and PM POSHAN first

key_terms.meaning: 2018 life-cycle strategy to cut anaemia with six groups and six actions.
Iron folic acid supplementation.
Deliberately raising a food's micronutrient content for public health benefit.
Breeding crops that contain more of a micronutrient.
Label mark required on fortified foods under reg. 7(2).

worked_example.title: Iron from fortified rice
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a person draws 5 kg of fortified rice a month, as in the NFSA entitlement. The deck gives 28 to 42.5 mg of iron per kg of rice.
steps: Lower bound: 5 × 28 = 140 mg a month.
Upper bound: 5 × 42.5 = 212.5 mg a month.
Per day at the low end: 140 ÷ 30 = 4.67 mg.
Per day at the high end: 212.5 ÷ 30 = 7.08 mg.
Adherence check: IFA for 100 days or more in pregnancy went from 44.1% to 54.9%, so 54.9 − 44.1 = 10.8 points.
worked_example.answer: Five kilograms of fortified rice would supply about 4.7 to 7.1 mg of iron a day, if the kernels are blended properly, and IFA compliance gained 10.8 points.

mistakes: Reading a rise in anaemia as proof that more iron is needed. The cut-off and blood sample debate matters.
Ignoring the sickle cell and thalassaemia advisory on iron-fortified food.
Assuming fortification works because the policy exists. Blending happens at the mill, so test the rice that reaches the household.

recall.q: What does 6x6x6 stand for?
recall.a: Six beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms.

recall.q: What share of rice in government schemes was fortified from March 2024?
recall.a: 100 percent.

recall.q: Which fortification is the clearest success?
recall.a: Salt iodisation, with 94.2 percent of households using iodised salt in NFHS-6.

recall.q: Which regulation sets the label rule?
recall.a: Reg. 7(2) of the FSSAI Fortification of Foods Regulations, 2018.

recall.q: What did the critics say about iron deficiency anaemia?
recall.a: If it is only about 10 percent, adding iron to everyone's staple has limited benefit.

sections.title: What works: the intervention evidence
sections.big_idea: Direct interventions save lives, counselling changes practice, cash helps a little and **household WASH did not move growth**.
in_plain_words: The 2013 Lancet model says ten direct interventions at 90 percent coverage cut under-five deaths by 15 percent but avert about a fifth of stunting. The 2021 update adds stronger evidence for several supplements. Coverage of the most vulnerable is the bigger problem.

Alive & Thrive moved feeding practices a great deal while stunting changed little in four years. Cash transfers help diets modestly, and large WASH trials found no household WASH effect on growth. Read nulls carefully: they apply to the intervention tested at the intensity tested.

children.label: Direct interventions
items: About a fifth of stunting averted

children.label: Household WASH
items: No growth effect in three trials

key_terms.meaning: Change in the intervention group minus change in comparison.
A trial finding no effect of the tested intervention.
Pooled estimate across many studies.
Effect in a controlled trial.
Effect in real delivery conditions.

worked_example.title: Read the Alive & Thrive numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the intensive group figures from slide 79 for exclusive breastfeeding, plus the SHINE stunting result.
steps: Change in the intensive group: 87.6 − 48.5 = 39.1 points.
The difference-in-differences effect was 36.2 points.
So the comparison group itself improved: 39.1 − 36.2 = 2.9 points.
SHINE nutrition arm: stunting went from 35% to 27%, so 35 − 27 = 8 points.
worked_example.answer: Breastfeeding rose 39.1 points, of which 36.2 is attributed to the programme. The comparison group gained 2.9, and SHINE's nutrition arm cut stunting 8 points.

mistakes: Citing a WASH null as evidence against all sanitation. The trials tested elementary household WASH only.
Judging a counselling project by stunting within two years. Practices move faster than height.
Assuming cash alone fixes diets. Effects are small and larger with counselling attached.

recall.q: What coverage did the 2013 Lancet model assume?
recall.a: 90 percent, for ten direct interventions in 34 countries.

recall.q: What happened to exclusive breastfeeding in Alive & Thrive's intensive group?
recall.a: It rose from 48.5 percent to 87.6 percent.

recall.q: What did cash transfer meta-analyses find on height-for-age?
recall.a: Small gains, +0.03 and +0.024 z.

recall.q: What did the three WASH trials find on growth?
recall.a: No household WASH effect on growth.

recall.q: How much cost did the 2013 model estimate?
recall.a: Int$9.6 billion a year in the 34 countries.

sections.title: South Asia compared
sections.big_idea: Neighbours show that **stunting can fall a point a year or more**, and that wasting and the second burden are the region's stubborn problems.
in_plain_words: Survey years differ by up to eight years, so treat the comparison as a snapshot. India has the highest wasting and underweight of the five countries, Sri Lanka has the lowest stunting, and Pakistan combines high stunting with rising overweight.

Bangladesh and Nepal nearly halved stunting in about fifteen years. Averages hide groups, such as Sri Lanka's estates and Pakistan's merged districts. Anaemia comparisons need caution because methods and years differ. Wasting moved least everywhere and starts in the first months of life.

key_terms.meaning: Demographic and Health Survey series, used for cross-country comparison.
DHS Program tool for comparing survey estimates.
Sri Lanka's plantation workforce and its families.
Newly merged districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Overweight and diet-related disease arriving beside undernutrition.

worked_example.title: Compare the pace of decline
worked_example.setup: Use the stunting rates and survey years from slide 87.
steps: Bangladesh 2007 to 2022: 43.2 − 23.6 = 19.6 points over 15 years.
Pace: 19.6 ÷ 15 = 1.31 points a year.
worked_example.answer: Bangladesh fell 1.3 points a year, Nepal 1.5 and India about 1.0 over a longer period, which supports the deck's 'a point a year or more'.

mistakes: Ranking countries on figures from surveys eight years apart.
Reading a national average as the experience of every group. Estates and merged districts sit far above it.
Comparing anaemia across countries without noting method and year differences.

recall.q: Which of the five countries has the lowest stunting?
recall.a: Sri Lanka.

recall.q: What was Pakistan's stunting rate in the NNS 2018?
recall.a: 40.2 percent.

recall.q: How much did Bangladesh's stunting fall and when?
recall.a: From 43.2 percent in 2007 to 23.6 percent in 2022.

recall.q: Where is wasting highest in Sri Lanka?
recall.a: Among infants aged 0-5 months, at 19 percent.

recall.q: Which four lessons does the slide give?
recall.a: Speed is possible, averages hide groups, wasting is stubborn and the second burden is arriving.

sections.title: Practical application: a practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: Diagnose first, design around entitlements and counselling, **measure with a named method**, and refer every child you find.
in_plain_words: The checklist has four steps: diagnose the form, age, cause and group, design around entitlements and counselling, measure on the WHO standard with confidence intervals, and protect with consent and referral. Match each programme aim to an indicator it can move within the funding period.

The decision table pairs diagnoses with responses, and the two worked examples show scale. A block's SAM caseload translates into NRC beds and a heavy screening load. A district target should follow the history of how fast stunting has fallen.

key_terms.meaning: Number of children with severe acute malnutrition at a point in time.
Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre for complicated SAM.
A goal for practices or access that the evidence links to growth.
Share affected at a single moment in time.
A known weakness, such as a definition changing in 2021.

worked_example.title: Size a block's screening load
worked_example.setup: Illustrative block of 8,000 children aged 6-59 months with 5% SAM, 12% MAM and 15% of SAM needing an NRC. Admissions stay 14 days.
steps: SAM children: 8,000 × 0.05 = 400.
MAM children: 8,000 × 0.12 = 960.
NRC admissions: 400 × 0.15 = 60.
Beds occupied on an average day: 60 × 14 ÷ 365 = 2.3.
Monthly MUAC screenings over a year: 8,000 × 12 = 96,000.
worked_example.answer: The block needs about 2 to 3 NRC beds but 96,000 screenings a year, so screening is the heavy workload.

mistakes: Setting a 10-point stunting target for three years. That is 3.3 points a year, against a history of 1 to 1.5.
Measuring without referring. The deck says never measure without acting.
Reading point prevalence as annual caseload. New cases arise through the year, so the caseload is several times larger.

recall.q: What are the four headings of the design checklist?
recall.a: Diagnose, design, measure and protect.

recall.q: What standard should you use for anthropometry?
recall.a: The WHO 2006 standard.

recall.q: What should a two-year feeding counselling project be judged on first?
recall.a: Feeding practices, with stunting only as a long-term aim.

recall.q: How fast does the deck say to set stunting targets?
recall.a: 1 to 1.5 points a year.

recall.q: What does the decision table suggest for high wasting under 6 months?
recall.a: Maternal nutrition, breastfeeding support, and SAM screening and referral.

sections.title: Bringing it together
sections.big_idea: Ten ideas tie the deck together: **three faces of malnutrition, debated levels, firm gradients, and law and platforms to act with**.
in_plain_words: The summary splits into understanding and acting. Malnutrition has three faces, stunting records history and wasting records crisis, causes run from diet to power, growth faltering starts in the womb, and India's levels are debated while its gradients are not.

On the action side, NFSA makes food and meals legal entitlements, Poshan 2.0 and related platforms deliver them, direct interventions save lives but most stunting needs wider change, and counselling moves practices faster than height. Check the latest round before quoting a number.

key_terms.meaning: A systematic difference between groups that holds under different yardsticks.
A right enforced in law, such as grain or a maternity benefit.
A programme that reaches people, such as Poshan 2.0 or PM POSHAN.
Linking schemes through one household list.
The eligible-to-effective chain used for monitoring.

worked_example.title: Match three diagnoses to responses
worked_example.setup: Apply the deck's decision table (slide 94) to three districts. No numbers are needed, only the rule that a diagnosis drives the response.
steps: District 1 has high wasting under six months: prioritise maternal nutrition, breastfeeding support and SAM screening and referral.
District 2 has a low minimum acceptable diet: prioritise complementary feeding counselling and eggs or pulses in rations.
District 3 has poor households missing entitlements: prioritise ration cards, NFSA grievance routes and PMMVY enrolment.
Most districts have more than one row, so rank by burden and by what the programme can reach.
worked_example.answer: Each diagnosis points to a different response, and a real district needs ranking across several rows, with the omitted rows named.

mistakes: Quoting a figure without the round, standard and method.
Treating the summary as new evidence. It restates what the earlier sections source.
Ignoring that NFHS, scheme periods and the DPDP timetable all move.

recall.q: What are the three faces of malnutrition?
recall.a: Undernutrition, hidden hunger and overweight.

recall.q: What does stunting record and what does wasting record?
recall.a: Stunting records history; wasting records crisis.

recall.q: Which delivery platforms does the summary name?
recall.a: Poshan 2.0, PM POSHAN, PMMVY and Anemia Mukt Bharat.

recall.q: What does counselling change fast and slowly?
recall.a: Practices change fast; height moves slowly.

recall.q: Where should you start in the Where next list?
recall.a: With the course that matches the gap you found in your own programme's cascade.

notes.2: This agenda shows how the deck moves: **what malnutrition is, how it is measured, why it happens, India's numbers, the debates, the law, programmes, micronutrients, evidence and the region**. Sections 11 and 12 are the application. If you design programmes, read Section 11 early and return to the evidence for the reasons behind each choice.
notes.4: Learn the three families first: **undernutrition, micronutrient deficiency, and overweight with diet-related disease**. A child can be of normal size and still be deficient, so size alone never shows the whole picture. UNICEF calls the combination the triple burden, and it can sit in one country, one district or one household.
notes.5: Read stunting as **a child's history in one number**: slow height growth records months or years of poor diet, infection and often a poor start before birth. India fell from 35.5 to 29.3 percent between rounds. The last line is the practitioner's rule: stunting describes populations, so one short child proves little.
notes.6: Wasting tracks **recent events**, such as a diarrhoeal episode, a lean season or a failed harvest, because weight responds within weeks. It is the form most tied to death, and a child both stunted and wasted faces a 4.8-fold rise in mortality. Treat severe wasting as an emergency for the individual child.
notes.7: The lesson here: underweight **mixes two stories**, so a fall in it cannot tell you whether a chronic or an acute problem improved. NFHS-6 shows the trap, with stunting falling six points while underweight barely moved. Report all three indicators together, and design around height-for-age and weight-for-height.
notes.8: Hidden hunger stays invisible without a blood or urine test, which is why surveys matter. Anaemia is the most widely measured sign, though it has many causes beyond iron. Hold on to the warning in the closing box: these are 2019-21 figures, and no newer anaemia numbers had been released as of October 2026.
notes.9: India now carries **thinness and overweight side by side**. In NFHS-6, more women are overweight or obese (30.7 percent) than thin (19.7 percent). Adult blood sugar is rising too. Child overweight under five fell to 1.3 percent, so the rise belongs to adults, and NFHS-5 showed it climbing steeply with wealth.
notes.10: The double burden can appear in one country, one district or one home. The design warning is that **adding calories alone can worsen the second burden**, for example a ration heavy in sugar and refined flour. Measure height and weight together and protect breastfeeding. Check every ration you design for diet quality as well as energy.
notes.11: These numbers explain why the topic matters: 45 percent of child deaths in 2011 were attributed to undernutrition, and survivors carry lower schooling and earnings. The slide says the figures are a decade old by design. Use the **latest Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates** whenever you need a current global count.
notes.13: Separate a **standard** from a **reference**. The WHO 2006 Child Growth Standards describe how children grow when their needs are met, using healthy, breastfed children from six countries including India. Estimates on different yardsticks cannot be compared, so recompute any long trend on the 2006 standard. NFHS-3, 4 and 5 all use it.
notes.14: A z-score counts **standard deviations from the healthy median**. A height-for-age score of −2.5 means two and a half deviations shorter than the median child of that age and sex. About 2.3 percent of a healthy population falls below −2 SD, so far higher prevalence signals a population problem. India's mean of −1.3 shows the whole distribution shifted down.
notes.15: A cut-off turns a continuous measure into yes or no. That helps with targets but loses information, since a child at −1.99 and one at −2.01 are nearly identical. Report **mean z-score and prevalence together**, and name the indicator, standard, age range and primary outcome in every proposal, because changing any of them changes the number.
notes.16: Measurement error enters at five places: age, position, equipment, measurer and recording. Use the table as a **field checklist**. Age is the easiest to forget, because rounded ages pile up at whole years, so ask for birth certificates, MCP cards or local event calendars. Children under 24 months are measured lying down.
notes.17: Data quality is **decided before fieldwork**. Standardise measurers on precision and accuracy, budget for rigid equipment, re-measure a subsample and look for digit preference. Then ask any programme survey to disclose its exclusions, as the CNNS does. The warning at the bottom: a programme's own baseline is where poor measurement most often creates a fake trend.
notes.18: MUAC is the **field screening tool**: a colour-coded tape, seconds to use, no scale or calculator. Memorise the cut-offs. Below 115 mm is severe, 115 to below 125 mm is moderate, and 125 mm or more is not acutely malnourished. MUAC and weight-for-height pick overlapping but different children, so the tool you choose changes your caseload.
notes.19: Anthropometry shows outcomes, while IYCF indicators show **one of the immediate causes**. Focus on three for children 6-23 months: minimum dietary diversity, minimum meal frequency and the minimum acceptable diet. The warning concerns definitions: NFHS-5 gives both four and five food groups in different places, so compare rounds only on one definition.
notes.20: Four decisions change an anaemia figure: which blood, which device, which adjustments and which cut-off. NFHS-5 used capillary blood and a portable device, while the CNNS used venous blood and laboratories. When two surveys disagree, **compare these four decisions before you compare the numbers**.
notes.21: Always analyse surveys with their weights, clusters and strata. The DHS weight must be divided by 1,000,000. Two traps: estimate subgroups on the full design instead of dropping records first, and treat district changes with care, because a **three-point change in one district may be noise**. Read the confidence interval before announcing progress.
notes.22: Poshan Tracker gives monthly, child-level, near real-time data across the Anganwadi network, so use it to **manage a programme**. It covers only enrolled children and is measured by workers judged on the results, so its prevalence figures are not comparable with NFHS. Use NFHS or CNNS to describe the population.
notes.23: Child nutrition data are personal data under the DPDP Act, and the duties arrive in stages. The core duties, including verifiable parental consent for children's data under s9, apply from 13 May 2027. **Write consent forms for that standard now** if your survey will still be running then. The research exemption never replaces ethics review.
notes.25: The 1990 framework sorts causes into **immediate, underlying and basic**. Learn the chain: diet and disease at the immediate level, food, care and health services beneath them, and social, economic and cultural processes at the base. Jonsson stresses that food, health and care are each necessary and none is sufficient alone.
notes.26: The 2020 framework asks **what has to be in place**: good diets and care, supportive food, practices and services, and an enabling environment of governance, resources and norms. Use the Indian block examples in the table as a design checklist. Moving from 'causes' to 'determinants' makes it useful for planning as well as diagnosis.
notes.27: Separate **nutrition-specific** actions, which act on immediate determinants, from **nutrition-sensitive** ones, which act on underlying and enabling determinants. The key figure: ten specific interventions at very high coverage avert only about a fifth of stunting. The rest depends on income, sanitation, women's status and food prices, which sit with other ministries.
notes.28: The first 1,000 days run from conception to the second birthday, when growth is fastest and damage hardest to reverse. The chart shows stunting climbing steeply from 6-8 to 18-23 months and then plateauing. Use that shape to argue that **prevention must start early**, well before a child turns two.
notes.29: Growth faltering often starts before birth. About 24.4 percent of infants under six months are already stunted, and 44 percent of children reported very small at birth are stunted. A child programme that begins at six months therefore starts late. Put **maternal and adolescent nutrition** inside a stunting strategy.
notes.30: Use the chart to see the gradient: a child whose mother has twelve or more years of schooling is about half as likely to be stunted as one whose mother has none. The slide cautions that these are associations, and that schooling, wealth and residence overlap, so **do not add the bars together**.
notes.31: Food alone is not enough when the gut is inflamed. Environmental enteric dysfunction, linked to faecal contamination, reduces absorption without obvious diarrhoea. This is the biological argument behind the sanitation debate in Section 5. Note that deworming reached only 30 percent of children 6-59 months before NFHS-5.
notes.33: Know the headline numbers: NFHS-6 shows **29.3 percent stunted, 19.0 wasted and 31.8 underweight**. Stunting fell 6.2 points while wasting and underweight barely moved. The fact sheet is provisional and gives main indicators only, so the breakdowns on this slide come from NFHS-5 until the NFHS-6 report is published.
notes.34: Read the chart as **two stories**. Stunting fell by about a point a year, then faster between the last two rounds, to 29.3 percent. Wasting stayed near 19 to 21 percent for almost two decades. All four rounds use the WHO standard, so the comparison is fair, although the NFHS-6 values are provisional.
notes.35: Use the state chart to see that stunting fell in almost every state. The highest in NFHS-6 are Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Meghalaya and Bihar, and the lowest are Puducherry, Chandigarh and Goa. Small samples sit behind the rises in Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Manipur was not surveyed.
notes.36: Anaemia rose between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5 in all three groups: children from 59 to 67 percent, women from 53 to 57 and men from 23 to 25. Child anaemia peaks at 80 percent at 12-17 months. These remain the latest figures as of October 2026, and **the measurement method is disputed**, as Section 5 explains.
notes.37: Scan the table for direction and size. Early breastfeeding and timely complementary food improved, but exclusive breastfeeding **fell about eight points** to 55.8 percent, which the slide calls a warning sign. Only 15.3 percent of children 6-23 months had an adequate diet. Check your own state's NFHS-6 sheet before drawing a local conclusion.
notes.38: The CNNS fills gaps that NFHS leaves. It measured **school-age children and adolescents**, used venous blood and laboratory methods, and assessed micronutrients directly. Use CNNS for micronutrients and older children, and NFHS for trends and district estimates of under-five anthropometry. It measured 112,316 children and adolescents in 30 states.
notes.39: Read the chart by age group. Adolescents carry the heaviest burden of zinc, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency. Iodine is the exception, with adequate status in all three groups, which the slide calls **the visible success of salt iodisation**. Tamil Nadu sat at the lower limit of excess intake.
notes.40: Anaemia and iron deficiency overlap but differ. In the CNNS, 41 percent of pre-school children were anaemic and 32 percent iron deficient, and adolescent girls show the sharpest gap with boys. The policy stake is that **iron treats only the iron-deficiency part**, which leads into the debate in Section 5. These are age-group figures; the all-ages figure is about 30 percent.
notes.41: Adolescents fall between programmes for under-fives and pregnant women. The table shows why it matters: 24 percent are thin, 40 percent of girls are anaemic and 40 percent of women aged 15-19 are thin. A thin, anaemic girl is **the mother whose baby is small at birth**. Anemia Mukt Bharat names adolescents 10-19 as a target group.
notes.43: Indian children are on average shorter than children in poorer sub-Saharan Africa, and four explanations compete. Use the table as a **map of the debate**: measurement, intra-household allocation, disease environment and maternal status. The slide says they are not mutually exclusive, so ask how much each accounts for and which one a programme can change.
notes.44: Learn both sides of the measurement argument. Panagariya argued that one global standard ignores genetic and environmental differences, while Pande attributes the gap to household choices. A third route keeps the standard and adjusts for parents. Be careful: **maternal height itself reflects the mother's own childhood nutrition**, so adjusting removes something programmes should care about.
notes.45: Jayachandran and Pande find that India's height gap relative to Africa **grows sharply with birth order**. They attribute it to favouritism toward eldest sons, and an approximate calculation suggests it explains over half the gap. The chart shows stunting rising across birth orders. Keep later-born children, and girls, in view when you plan.
notes.46: Spears links sanitation and height: across 140 country-years, sanitation alone explains 54 percent of the variation in child height. District evidence from India points the same way. Remember the limit the authors flag: these analyses are **observational and ecological**, so confounding remains possible. Section 9 shows what randomised trials found.
notes.47: The 2023 case for customising the WHO standard rests on healthy Indian children whose mean z-scores sat below zero. Weigh the case against: a 'healthy' sample in a stunted population may itself be growth-constrained. The practical advice is to **report on the WHO 2006 standard** and note the debate. Trends measured on one standard are unaffected.
notes.48: The cut-off debate asks whether WHO haemoglobin thresholds overstate anaemia. Sachdev's healthy-subsample cut-offs cut CNNS prevalence from 30.0 to 10.8 percent. WHO's own 2024 guideline lowered the threshold for children aged 6-23 months to 10.5 g/dL. Treat the **cut-off as part of the result** whenever you quote an anaemia figure.
notes.49: Same disease, two methods, two answers. NFHS uses capillary blood and reports 67.1 percent of children anaemic, while venous CNNS blood puts it at about 30 percent (30.7 in Kurpad and Sachdev, 30.0 in Sachdev and colleagues). They argue that policy should rest on the cause of anaemia, and that the NFHS figure **might be an overestimate**.
notes.50: This table is a reusable method for any measurement debate: ask about the yardstick, the sample, what changes if the critic is right, the policy stake and what does not change. The key insight is that **critics mostly challenge levels, while gradients survive every yardstick**. Design for the gradients and revisit levels later.
notes.52: Follow the legal path. A 2001 petition in PUCL v Union of India turned food schemes into entitlements through interim orders, and the National Food Security Act 2013 wrote much of that into law. The slide says sections 4 to 6 and Schedule II now carry what the courts demanded. The root is the **Article 21 right to life**.
notes.53: Memorise the core entitlement: **5 kg per person per month** for a priority household and 35 kg per household for Antyodaya, at Rs 3, 2 and 1 per kg for rice, wheat and coarse grains. Coverage reaches up to 75 percent of rural and 50 percent of urban people. The 2027 Census will reopen each State's coverage numbers.
notes.54: Sections 4 to 6 turn the right to food into **life-cycle entitlements**: a meal for pregnant women and lactating mothers, maternity benefit of at least Rs 6,000, meals for children from 6 months to 6 years, and a mid-day meal up to class VIII. Use the Schedule II table to check calories and protein against what a centre serves.
notes.55: PMGKAY made foodgrain **free** for about 81.35 crore people for five years from 1 January 2024, at an estimated cost of Rs 11.80 lakh crore. Free cereal guarantees calories but does less for diversity, which is why s12(2)(f) asks for diversification of PDS commodities. Pair this slide with the dietary diversity data in Section 4.
notes.56: Two provisions with teeth: s13 puts the ration card in the **eldest woman's name**, and s8 gives a claim to a food security allowance when grain is not supplied. Few beneficiaries know either. The slide suggests a ration card audit as a first nutrition-sensitive step: whose name is on the card, and was the allowance paid?
notes.57: Know the escalation ladder: internal grievance redressal (s14), the District Grievance Redressal Officer (s15) and the State Food Commission (s16), backed by social audits (s28), vigilance committees (s29) and penalties (s33). The slide adds that these exist on paper in every State but **function unevenly**. Use the table to tell a complainant where to go first.
notes.58: The PDS has been digitised at scale: 99.9 percent of ration cards are Aadhaar-seeded and 99.8 percent of shops use ePoS devices. **One Nation One Ration Card** lets migrant workers draw rations where they work. Section 12 of the Act lists the reform options, including cash transfers, which began in Chandigarh and Puducherry in 2015.
notes.59: Use the table to see that each PDS reform has a trade-off, and note what to measure on each side. The slide's memorable test: for any reform, ask **what happens to the poorest household in the worst-run block**, since that is where nutrition is decided. The Act allows cash or coupons only as the Centre prescribes.
notes.61: ICDS began on 2 October 1975 and built the Anganwadi network. The 2021-22 Budget merged Anganwadi Services, the Scheme for Adolescent Girls and POSHAN Abhiyaan into Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0. Remember its **three verticals**: nutrition support, early childhood care and education, and Anganwadi infrastructure.
notes.62: Anganwadis give supplementary nutrition to children 6 months to 6 years, pregnant women, lactating mothers and adolescent girls, under norms revised in January 2023 toward diet diversity. The design question is **take home ration or hot cooked meal**. Face recognition for rations adds a new exclusion point, so monitor who is turned away.
notes.63: POSHAN Abhiyaan set targets and brought more than 26 ministries under one framework. Check the scorecard: the mission aimed for **25 percent stunting by 2022**, while NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 found 35.5 and 29.3 percent. Its annual target of 2 points does not reach that ambition: it gives 6 points over three years against 13.4 needed.
notes.64: The law sets a floor of not less than Rs 6,000 in maternity benefit, and PMMVY delivers it by direct cash transfer. Face authentication became mandatory for new enrolments from 21 May 2025. For any scheme, ask whether **amount, eligibility and documentation** meet the s4(b) floor for every pregnant woman the Act covers.
notes.65: PM POSHAN is the school meal, formerly the Mid-Day Meal Scheme. Its approved period ended with 2025-26, so **check the current approval** before quoting outlay or coverage. The legal entitlement does not lapse, because it sits in NFSA s5(1)(b). The right to a cooked meal was won through PUCL v Union of India.
notes.66: Nutrition is split across ministries: Women and Child Development, Health, Food and Public Distribution, Education, FSSAI and the States. POSHAN Abhiyaan exists because those schemes did not connect. At district level the practical test is whether the **Anganwadi Worker, ASHA, ANM and fair price shop dealer share one household list** and meet on a fixed day.
notes.67: Follow the cascade: eligible, enrolled, served, consumed, effective. **Each arrow is a place to lose people**, from migrant families who miss enrolment to take home rations shared in the household. The slide's warning: monitoring that counts only the first two steps will report success while children stay short.
notes.69: Anemia Mukt Bharat is organised as 6x6x6: six beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms. Learn the three lists separately. The groups run from children 6-59 months to lactating women, and the interventions include prophylactic iron folic acid, deworming, behaviour change and digital testing. **Iron supply is one lever of six.**
notes.70: Supplements work only if they are **taken**, so track doses consumed as well as doses distributed. IFA for 100 days or more in pregnancy rose from 44.1 to 54.9 percent. The slide's district advice: test reliably, find the iron-deficient share, treat severe anaemia in pregnancy urgently, and screen for haemoglobin disorders before universal iron.
notes.71: Fortification regulation in brief: the 2018 rules require mandatory fortification to rest on public health evidence, set label rules including the +F logo, and require an advisory on iron-fortified food for thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. Use the table as the **legal checklist** when you audit a product's label.
notes.72: Fortified rice moved fast: a pilot in 15 states, a 2021 announcement, then **100 percent of rice in government schemes by March 2024** and supply extended to December 2028. The kernels carry iron, folic acid and vitamin B12. Blending happens at the mill, so what reaches the household depends on mixing quality.
notes.73: Weigh the two cases. The government cites a WHO meta-analysis that rice fortification can reduce the risk of iron deficiency by 35 percent. Critics note that if iron deficiency anaemia is only about 10 percent the benefit is limited, and that sickle cell patients are advised against iron. In practice, **measure whether kernels reach the household** and track iron status.
notes.74: Iodised salt is the clearest success, and the slide explains why: one cheap nutrient, a vehicle everyone eats in steady amounts, few producers to regulate and a deficiency the nutrient alone corrects. **Iron in rice meets fewer of those conditions.** NFHS-6 found 94.2 percent of households using iodised salt.
notes.75: Eat Right India addresses the second half of the double burden: food safety, fats, sugar and salt, including a campaign to remove industrial trans fats. It matters most for urban and richer groups, where 42.8 percent of urban women are overweight or obese. A **double-duty plan needs child undernutrition programmes and food environment action together**.
notes.77: The 2013 Lancet modelling says ten direct interventions at 90 percent coverage cut under-five deaths by 15 percent but avert only about a fifth of stunting. Draw two lessons: **coverage is the binding constraint** for saving lives, and most stunting needs wider change in women's status, food systems and social protection.
notes.78: The 2021 update strengthens several items: antenatal multiple micronutrient supplements, supplementary food, community management of acute malnutrition and small-quantity lipid-based supplements. Look at the last row: **malaria prevention, preconception care and WASH promotion** bring nutritional benefits too. The authors stress that coverage of the most vulnerable is the bigger problem.
notes.79: Alive & Thrive shows **behaviour change can move practices fast**: exclusive breastfeeding rose from 48.5 to 87.6 percent in the intensive group. Stunting fell in both groups by similar amounts within four years. Set targets accordingly: judge counselling first on feeding practices and treat height as a longer-term aim.
notes.80: Adding nutrition to antenatal care raised the share of women eating five or more food groups by 30 points and exclusive breastfeeding by 31. The slide credits **coverage of home visits**, with more than 90 percent visited. Poshan Tracker plans 23 structured home visits, but whether they happen and what is said will decide its worth.
notes.81: Read the two meta-analyses as a pattern: cash improves diets and reduces stunting, but **by small amounts**. Height-for-age z-scores rose only 0.03 and 0.024. The 2022 review found that well-targeted behaviour change communication alongside cash improved height. For India, cash helps diets, and it helps more with counselling attached.
notes.82: The three trials tell a consistent story: household WASH produced **no growth effect**, while the nutrition arm raised length-for-age by 0.13 to 0.25 z. Combining WASH with nutrition did not add growth beyond nutrition alone. Note what was tested: elementary household WASH, which is different from community-wide sanitation.
notes.83: Learn the lesson in the last paragraph. A null result is strong evidence about **the intervention tested at the intensity tested**, and weak evidence about a different intervention with the same label. Before you cite a trial to start or stop a programme, check that your programme is the thing the trial evaluated.
notes.84: Biofortification breeds nutrients into the crop, so no processing step is needed. In Maharashtra, iron-biofortified pearl millet improved iron status in 246 children. Mind the limit: **efficacy in a feeding trial** differs from effectiveness when farmers must choose to grow the crop and households to eat it.
notes.86: Compare with care, because survey years differ by up to eight years. The contrast the slide draws: Sri Lanka has the lowest stunting but wasting close to India's, and India has the **highest wasting** of the five. Check the survey year in the source line before you quote a country ranking.
notes.87: Bangladesh and Nepal each nearly halved stunting in about fifteen years: Bangladesh from 43.2 to 23.6 percent and Nepal from 49.3 to 24.8. India fell from 48.0 to 29.3. The slide describes Bangladesh's decline as a rapid **secular trend**, so improvement can come from forces outside any single programme.
notes.88: Pakistan shows high stunting (40.2 percent) beside a rising second burden: overweight in children under five rose from 5 to 9.5 percent, and 37.8 percent of women are overweight or obese. Note the **within-country range**, from 32.6 percent stunting in Islamabad to 48.3 percent in the merged districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
notes.89: Sri Lanka has good services and strong breastfeeding, yet wasting of 15.1 percent sits close to India's. Wasting is highest among infants aged 0-5 months, so **birthweight and maternal nutrition** matter as much as complementary feeding. A good national average also hides a plantation-sector stunting rate of 32 percent.
notes.90: Take four lessons from the region: speed is possible, averages hide groups, wasting is stubborn and a second burden is arriving. The anaemia table needs care because methods and years differ, and STATcompiler shows no Bangladesh anaemia estimate after 2011. Use it for **orders of magnitude** only.
notes.92: Use this checklist in four steps: diagnose, design, measure, protect. In the design block, link to entitlements first and **pair any food or cash with counselling**. The last line under Protect is a rule to repeat: refer every SAM child you find, and never measure without acting.
notes.93: Choose an indicator the programme can plausibly move within the funding period. The table pairs each aim with an indicator, a source and a pitfall, such as the **definition change in 2021**. Remember the example: a two-year counselling project should be judged on feeding practices first, and on stunting only as a long-term aim.
notes.94: Use the decision table to match diagnosis to response, for instance **maternal nutrition and breastfeeding support** for high wasting under six months, or venous testing and haemoglobinopathy screening when anaemia is high and the cause uncertain. Most districts need more than one row, so rank by burden and reach, and say which rows you leave out.
notes.95: Work this example through with a pencil. The lesson is in the last paragraph: prevalence is a snapshot, so the **annual caseload is several times the point prevalence**. Screening is the largest workload, and it falls on Anganwadi Workers who also run the centre. Budget tapes, training and supervision before promising coverage.
notes.96: Target-setting needs history. India's stunting fell about one point a year between NFHS-3 and NFHS-4 and about 1.5 a year to NFHS-6, so a 10-point drop in three years would be unprecedented. Commit to **process targets** that the evidence links to growth, and set stunting at 1 to 1.5 points a year.
notes.98: These ten ideas are the deck's summary. Read the left column as understanding and the right as action. The final paragraph matters for accuracy: **NFHS, scheme periods and the DPDP timetable all move**, so check the latest round and the latest approval before you quote a number.
notes.99: This slide maps the gaps you may find to the next course. Health and early childhood courses cover antenatal care, child development, epidemiology and counselling, and the methods courses cover sampling, trials, delivery cascades and data protection. Follow the closing advice and start with the course that matches **the gap in your own cascade**.
